opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the next twelve months will look less like a single dramatic leap and more like a steady compounding of things we've already seen start to work.

The biggest driver, in my view, is still post-training, especially reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We've learned that if you can check whether an answer is right, in math, in code, in certain kinds of tool use, you can push models a lot further than pretraining alone would suggest. Over the next year I expect labs to keep expanding the set of domains where they can construct those reward signals, and to get much better at training models to work over long horizons: running for hours, calling tools, recovering from mistakes, and actually finishing a task instead of just producing a plausible-looking first draft.

So the word I'd keep an eye on is "agents," but in a more grounded sense than the hype. Coding agents are the clearest example. They've gone from autocomplete to something that can take a ticket and open a pull request, and I think within a year a meaningful share of routine software work at a lot of companies will be initiated or done by these systems, with humans reviewing. Outside of code, progress will be slower and messier, because the environments are less clean and the rewards are harder to define.

On the model side, I'd expect continued gains at the frontier, but also a lot of the action happening in efficiency: smaller models that are surprisingly capable, better inference-time compute tradeoffs, and costs per unit of capability continuing to fall quickly. That matters as much as raw benchmark scores, because it determines what people can actually deploy.

I also care a lot about open models, and I think that ecosystem will stay very competitive. Chinese labs in particular have been releasing strong open-weight models, and that puts real pressure on the U.S. side to keep investing in open research. Whether we get a healthy, transparent open ecosystem or one that's mostly dependent on a few releases from abroad is, to me, one of the more important questions for the year ahead.

And finally, evaluation is going to be a bottleneck. Many of the benchmarks we relied on are saturated, so a lot of the debate over the next year will be about how we even measure progress, especially for agentic, long-running tasks where the interesting failures are subtle. I'd expect the models to keep surprising us on some things and be frustratingly brittle on others, and that unevenness is probably the most realistic forecast I can give.

r001.rationale: The response highlights agents and predicts wider use of coding agents, but does not predict that a new agentic product will become a major focus of attention.

r002.rationale: It expects long-horizon agent capabilities to improve and says progress outside code will be slower and messier, but does not characterize complex agentic workflows as being at a very early stage.

r003.rationale: The response expects steady compounding rather than a dramatic leap; it does not express uncertainty about whether progress will follow its current trajectory or change through a breakthrough.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll give you my honest read, with the caveat that anyone who tells you they know exactly what the next twelve months look like is overselling.

The first thing I expect is that the frontier keeps moving, but the shape of the progress changes. The last couple of years were defined by scaling pretraining, then by reasoning models and reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks. That RL recipe still has a lot of headroom, so I expect the biggest gains to show up in agentic behavior: models that can run for hours on a coding task, use tools reliably, recover from their own mistakes, and finish things end to end rather than produce a draft for a human to fix. The benchmarks that matter will shift from "can it answer this question" to "can it complete this job."

Second, I think the gap between closed and open models stays roughly where it is, maybe six to twelve months, but the open ecosystem gets a lot more interesting. Chinese labs have been shipping very strong open weights, and that pressure forces American labs and the research community to respond. I spend a lot of my time on open models, and the question I care about is whether we get genuinely open training recipes, data, and RL environments, not just weights. I'm cautiously optimistic that we see more of that, partly because the people building it realize the knowledge is getting concentrated in a handful of companies.

Third, the economics get real. Inference costs keep falling, but the top labs are spending enormous amounts on compute and the revenue has to catch up. I expect a lot of pricing experimentation, more specialization, and probably some consolidation among smaller players. The "one model that does everything for everyone" story gives way to a mix of frontier systems for hard problems and smaller, cheaper models deployed widely.

What I don't expect is a sudden discontinuity. Progress has been fast and steady rather than a single jump, and I think that continues. The hard parts over the next year are less about raw capability and more about reliability, evaluation, and figuring out what these systems are actually for in the real world. That's slower, less glamorous work, but it's where the value gets created.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest shift over the next twelve months will be from models that answer questions to systems that can actually carry out tasks. Coding is probably the clearest example: you give a system a problem, and it can work through the code, run tests, and iterate. But there’s a big gap between doing that in a compelling demo and doing it reliably enough that you can delegate work every day.

I’d expect more progress from training models to reason through problems and giving them more computation at inference time. That creates an interesting tradeoff: when is a better answer worth waiting longer or paying more? A lot of the product work will be figuring out when to use that extra effort.

I also expect capable models to become cheaper and more widely available, including open models. But I’m less confident about any particular breakthrough or timeline. The thing I’d watch is how much useful work these systems can complete without someone stepping in. That’s a much more meaningful measure of progress than whether a chatbot sounds a little smarter.

r002.rationale: It describes a gap between demos and reliable daily delegation, but does not characterize complex agentic workflows as being at a very early stage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next twelve months will be less about a single dramatic breakthrough and more about making the capabilities we already see actually useful. Models will get better at coding, reasoning through problems, and using tools, but the question is how reliably they can do those things when somebody isn’t watching every step.

Coding is one of the clearest places to watch because you can test whether the output works. I expect more progress on systems that can take a task, make changes, run tests, and iterate. That doesn’t mean they can suddenly replace an engineer; it means the division of work starts to change.

I’d also watch open models and the cost of running them. If strong capabilities become much cheaper and easier to customize, that opens up a lot of applications. But I’m cautious about precise timelines. A compelling demo and something you trust to handle your work every day are still very different milestones.
